weekly.title: hexdump(1) and a float dissector
weekly.brief:
Build two small command-line tools, one in C and one in Python, that make the
machine's representation of data visible.

**Tool 1 — `hd`.** A hexdump clone. Read bytes from a file or stdin, print 16 per line as
two-digit hex plus an ASCII gutter, with the byte offset in hex at the left. Add `-e` to
print the same buffer interpreted as little-endian and big-endian 16/32/64-bit integers,
side by side, so the endianness difference is a thing you *see* rather than a fact you
recite. Add `-s N`/`-n N` for offset and length. Handle a file that is not a multiple of
16 bytes, a zero-length file, and binary that contains NUL and 0xFF.

**Tool 2 — `f64`.** Give it a decimal literal; it prints the IEEE 754 binary64 sign,
exponent and significand fields in binary, the exact decimal value of the stored double
(use Python's `Decimal` or `fractions.Fraction` — the true value, not a rounded print),
the ULP at that magnitude, and the two neighbouring representable doubles. Then add a
`--sum` mode that takes a list of numbers and reports naive left-to-right sum, sorted-
ascending sum, pairwise sum and Kahan sum, with the exact error of each against the
rational sum.

**Why.** Every later week assumes you can look at a byte and know what it is. This week is
where "0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3" stops being trivia and becomes an arithmetic fact you can derive
on paper. It is also the first repo, so it establishes the shape of every submission:
README, tests, a Makefile, and CI that runs on push.

**Done looks like.** `make test` is green on a clean clone. `./hd /bin/ls | head` matches
`xxd` byte-for-byte on the first 4 KiB (diff it in CI). `f64 0.1` prints the exact value
`0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625`. The README shows three
worked examples and states, in your own words, why the sorted sum is not always the most
accurate one.

acceptance.text: `./hd` output is byte-identical to `xxd` for at least three test files including one empty and one containing NUL bytes; the comparison runs in CI.
`hd -e` prints the same 8 bytes as both little-endian and big-endian u64 and the two differ for a non-palindromic input.
`f64 0.1` prints the exact decimal expansion of the stored double, not a rounded rendering.
`f64 --sum` reports naive, sorted, pairwise and Kahan sums with exact errors, and there is a documented input where naive beats sorted.
The C tool compiles with `-Wall -Wextra -Werror -fsanitize=address,undefined` and the test suite runs clean under both sanitizers.
README states the ULP at 1.0, at 2^53, and at 0.1, each computed by the tool and checked by hand.

levels.5: Matches for empty, short-tail and binary inputs, and the comparison is automated in CI.

weekly.title: A reproducible toolchain and a bash suite that does not break
weekly.brief:
Build the environment you will live in for the next six months, and prove it works
on a machine that is not yours.

**Part 1 — `devbox`.** One repository that bootstraps your whole working environment from
a clean Ubuntu container: compilers, Python with a pinned virtualenv, gdb, perf, ripgrep,
jq, and the dotfiles you actually want. It must be idempotent — running it twice changes
nothing the second time — and it must be tested by a CI job that starts from
`ubuntu:24.04`, runs the bootstrap, and then runs a smoke script that compiles a C file,
runs pytest, and prints tool versions.

**Part 2 — `logkit`.** A small suite of bash tools over a synthetic log file you generate
(at least 200 MB, with deliberately nasty rows: spaces in fields, embedded newlines in
quoted values, a UTF-8 field, an empty field, and a filename containing a newline in a
companion directory listing). Write: a top-N-by-count reporter, a per-minute rate
histogram, a p50/p95/p99 latency extractor, and a "find every file whose name breaks your
loop" checker. Every script starts with a safety preamble, passes ShellCheck with zero
warnings, uses `IFS=` and `read -r`, and handles filenames with `find -print0 | xargs -0`.

**Part 3 — the git muscle.** In a scratch repo, deliberately create and then resolve: a
merge conflict in the middle of a hunk, a rebase that must be aborted, a commit recovered
from the reflog after a hard reset, and a bisect run that finds a planted bug in a 40-commit
history. Record each as a transcript.

**Why.** Every following week costs less if the toolchain is not a variable. And the
research is explicit that public repo history is evidence of process, not just product —
this week is where you start producing a history worth reading.

**Done looks like.** A stranger runs one command in a container and ends up with your
environment. `shellcheck -S style *.sh` is silent. The bisect transcript names the exact
commit.

acceptance.text: CI starts from a bare `ubuntu:24.04` image, runs the bootstrap end to end, and the smoke script passes.
Running the bootstrap twice produces no diff in the second run's change log (idempotence is asserted, not claimed).
`shellcheck -S style` reports zero findings across every script in the repo, checked in CI.

The log suite gives correct answers on the nasty-row fixture, including the quoted-newline row and the space-in-field row; a naive `for f in $(...)` version is included in the repo and shown to give the wrong answer.
p95 computed by your awk script matches a numpy reference to within one rank position on the fixture.
Four git transcripts (conflict, aborted rebase, reflog recovery, bisect) are committed, and the bisect one names the planted commit hash.

levels.1: Second run errors or silently re-installs.
levels.3: Second run succeeds; idempotence asserted by hand.
levels.5: A CI job runs it twice and fails the build if the second run changes state.

weekly.title: Data structures in C, with a benchmark that changes your mind
weekly.brief:
Implement, from scratch in C, the five structures that everything else is built on,
then measure them until the asymptotics stop being the interesting part.

**Implement.** (1) A dynamic array with a documented growth factor and an amortised-append
argument you can state. (2) A hash table with open addressing, linear probing, tombstones,
and a resize at a load factor you choose and justify. (3) A singly linked list. (4) A
binary search tree, plus a deliberately unbalanced insertion order that makes it degenerate.
(5) A binary min-heap with `sift_up`/`sift_down` and an O(n) `heapify`.

All five behind one small `Map`/`Seq` interface so the benchmark harness can swap
implementations. Every one gets a property test: insert N random keys, delete a random
half, assert every survivor is findable and every deleted key is not, for N up to 10^6, with
a fixed seed printed on failure.

**Measure.** Build a harness that reports operations per second and, using `perf stat`,
cycles, instructions, cache misses and branch misses per operation. Then answer four
questions with data, not intuition:
- At what N does the hash table beat the BST for lookup, and why is that N not 1?
- What does growth factor 1.5 vs 2.0 do to total memory touched and to realloc count for
  10^7 appends?
- How much slower is the linked list than the array for a full traversal at N = 10^6, and
  what does the cache-miss counter say about why?
- What does the degenerate BST cost, and what does the recursion-depth measurement say
  about stack space?

**Why.** This is the week the phrase "constants win in practice" acquires a number. The
benchmark, not the code, is the artifact.

**Done looks like.** A plot per question, generated by a script from committed CSV, with
the machine, compiler flags, and run-to-run variance stated. No plot without error bars.

acceptance.text: All five structures pass the randomised property test at N = 10^6 with a printed seed, under ASan and UBSan.
Valgrind or ASan reports zero leaks after a full insert/delete/free cycle on every structure.
The harness emits CSV; plots are regenerated from that CSV by a committed script, not pasted images.
The array-vs-list traversal comparison reports cache misses per element from `perf stat`, and the ratio is discussed.
The hash-table-vs-BST crossover N is reported with the measurement's variance across at least five runs.
The write-up states CPU model, compiler version, optimisation flags and whether frequency scaling was pinned.

rubric.criterion: Correctness under adversarial and random input

levels.1: Only hand-written unit tests; tombstone or resize path untested.
levels.3: Randomised tests pass at moderate N.
levels.5: Randomised tests at 10^6 plus a deliberately adversarial key set that forces clustering, all under sanitizers.

rubric.criterion: Memory is correctly owned and released

levels.3: No leaks on the happy path.
levels.5: No leaks on any path including failed insert and mid-resize failure, proven by a sanitizer run in CI.

rubric.criterion: Benchmark methodology is defensible

levels.1: Single run, no variance, no environment stated.
levels.3: Repeated runs with a mean reported.
levels.5: Repeats with variance, environment fully stated, warm-up discarded, and one named source of measurement error addressed.

rubric.criterion: Conclusions follow from the counters, not from theory

levels.5: Hardware counters are used to explain a result that the asymptotics alone would get wrong.

rubric.criterion: One interface, swappable implementations

levels.1: Each structure has its own ad-hoc API.
levels.3: A shared header exists but the harness special-cases implementations.
levels.5: Harness is implementation-agnostic; adding a sixth structure requires no harness change.

weekly.title: Linear algebra you can compute, and the errors it hides
weekly.brief:
Write a small dense linear algebra library in numpy-free Python (lists and loops are
fine; speed is not the point) and then use numpy only as the oracle you check against.

**Implement.** LU with partial pivoting and a solver for `Ax = b`; Gram-Schmidt (classical
and modified) and QR; power iteration for the dominant eigenpair; the Rayleigh quotient;
a Jacobi eigenvalue routine for symmetric matrices; and PCA implemented twice — once via
the covariance matrix's eigendecomposition and once via the SVD of the centred data
matrix. Include vector and matrix norms, and a condition number estimate.

**Then break it.** Build the Hilbert matrix `H_n` for n = 4, 8, 12, 16. Solve `H_n x = b`
for a known `x`, and plot relative forward error against the condition number. The line you
get is the standard model of floating-point error made visible: error grows roughly like
`kappa(A)` times unit roundoff. Do the same experiment with classical vs modified
Gram-Schmidt on a deliberately ill-conditioned basis and show that classical loses
orthogonality while modified does not — measure it as `||Q^T Q - I||`.

**And prove one thing by hand.** Pick one identity — the normal equations, or that PCA
directions are the right singular vectors of the centred data — and write the derivation on
a blank page from memory, then check the algebra numerically on random matrices at three
sizes.

**Why.** Every later week (autodiff, attention, GEMM, quantisation) is linear algebra with
error bars. Doing it once by hand, with the error measured rather than assumed, is what
makes the later weeks fast.

**Done looks like.** Every routine agrees with `numpy.linalg` to a stated tolerance across
100 random matrices per size. Two plots: forward error vs condition number, and loss of
orthogonality vs step. One hand-written derivation, photographed or typeset.

acceptance.text: Every routine is checked against `numpy.linalg` over at least 100 random matrices at three sizes, with the tolerance stated and justified in terms of unit roundoff.
The Hilbert experiment plots relative forward error against condition number for n = 4, 8, 12, 16 and the slope is compared to the `kappa * u` prediction.
Classical and modified Gram-Schmidt are compared by `||Q^T Q - I||` on the same ill-conditioned input and the gap is at least three orders of magnitude.
PCA via covariance eigendecomposition and PCA via SVD agree on the principal directions up to sign, and the sign ambiguity is handled explicitly.
One derivation is produced from a blank page and is included as an image or typeset appendix; its result is then verified numerically.
Power iteration reports the number of iterations to a fixed tolerance and the ratio of the top two eigenvalues, and the two are shown to be related.

rubric.criterion: Numerical agreement with the oracle is quantified, not asserted

levels.1: Agreement checked by eye or with `==`.
levels.3: A fixed tolerance is used across tests.
levels.5: Tolerance is derived from unit roundoff and problem size, and failures at large condition number are explained rather than loosened away.

rubric.criterion: The conditioning experiment supports a quantitative claim

levels.5: Measured slope compared against the predicted `kappa * u` bound, with the discrepancy discussed.

rubric.criterion: Gram-Schmidt comparison isolates the variable

levels.1: Different inputs used for the two variants.
levels.5: Same input and seed, loss measured per column so the accumulation is visible, and re-orthogonalisation tested as a third arm.

rubric.criterion: The hand derivation is genuinely from memory and is correct

levels.3: Produced from memory with gaps filled after.
levels.5: Produced blank-page, correct, and the numerical check uses cases that would catch a sign or transpose error.

rubric.criterion: Code is readable as mathematics

levels.1: Index soup, no comments tying code to notation.
levels.3: Named variables match the usual notation.
levels.5: Each routine's docstring states the input assumptions, the output guarantee, and the failure mode when they are violated.

weekly.title: A reverse-mode autodiff engine and the MLP it trains
weekly.brief:
Write a scalar-then-tensor reverse-mode automatic differentiation engine from nothing,
and use it to train a real classifier — no PyTorch anywhere in the training path.

**Stage 1 — scalars.** A `Value` type holding data, grad, a backward closure and its
parents. Support `+ - * / **`, `exp`, `log`, `tanh`, `relu`. Build the topological sort and
the backward pass. Verify every operator against a central finite difference at three
inputs each, and state the step size you chose and why (the `h ~ eps^(1/3)` argument for
central differences).

**Stage 2 — tensors.** Redo it over numpy arrays with broadcasting, and get the broadcast
gradient right — this is where most implementations quietly break. Implement `matmul`, `sum`,
`mean`, `reshape`, `transpose`, softmax and cross-entropy fused into one numerically stable
node (subtract the row max; show the unstable version overflowing on a logit of 800).

**Stage 3 — train something.** An MLP on Fashion-MNIST or CIFAR-10, CPU only. Implement
SGD, momentum, and AdamW yourself. Show, with plots: the effect of Xavier vs He vs
all-zeros initialisation on the first-layer gradient norms; the dying-ReLU phenomenon and
its rescue; what weight decay does when applied as L2-in-the-gradient versus decoupled;
and a learning-rate sweep that finds the edge of divergence.

**Why.** Backprop is the single mechanism the entire rest of the ML half of this curriculum
sits on. Deriving it and then hitting the broadcast-gradient bug yourself is worth more
than reading it five times.

**Done looks like.** `gradcheck` passes for every op to 1e-6 relative. The MLP reaches a
stated accuracy on a held-out split. Four plots, each answering one question asked above.

acceptance.text: Central-difference gradient check passes to 1e-6 relative error for every implemented operator, including the broadcasting cases, and the check is a test in CI.
A broadcast case (e.g. `(32,10) + (10,)`) has its gradient summed back to the correct shape, and a deliberately wrong version is included in the tests as a negative control.
The fused softmax-cross-entropy is stable at logit magnitude 800 while the naive version overflows; both are shown.
The MLP trains on CPU to a stated held-out accuracy with the exact command, seed and wall-clock time recorded.
Initialisation comparison plots first-layer gradient norm at step 0 for Xavier, He and zeros, and the variance argument is stated.
AdamW is shown to differ from Adam-plus-L2 on the same run, and the difference is explained in terms of where the decay enters.

levels.3: Gradcheck passes for tensor ops in the shapes actually used.
levels.5: Gradcheck passes for shapes that exercise every broadcast axis, with a negative control proving the test would catch the bug.

rubric.criterion: Numerical stability is engineered, not stumbled into

levels.5: Max-subtraction present, the unstable variant retained and demonstrated, and the log-sum-exp identity written out.

rubric.criterion: Training experiments isolate one variable each

levels.3: One variable per run, single seed.
levels.5: One variable per run, three seeds, bands plotted rather than lines.

rubric.criterion: Optimiser implementations match their definitions

levels.1: Copied without bias correction or with the wrong epsilon placement.
levels.5: Correct, plus a unit test that reproduces a hand-computed two-step update for each optimiser.

weekly.title: CS144 part one: byte stream, reassembler, TCP receiver
weekly.brief:
Start Stanford CS144's lab sequence and build the receive half of a TCP implementation
in C++ from scratch. This is the first of two weeks; week 7 finishes the job and puts your
stack on the real internet.

**Build.** (1) `ByteStream` — a reliable in-order byte pipe with a capacity, write/read,
end-of-input and error states. Get the capacity accounting exactly right; almost every
later bug traces back to it. (2) `Reassembler` — accepts substrings that arrive out of
order, overlapping, duplicated, or beyond the window, and pushes bytes into the stream in
order, storing only what it must. Track "bytes pending" and prove it never exceeds capacity.
(3) `TCPReceiver` — turn 32-bit wrapping sequence numbers into 64-bit absolute stream
indices and back, handle SYN and FIN occupying one sequence number each, and produce the
correct ackno and window size.

The wraparound conversion is the part that will humble you: the same 32-bit seqno recurs
every 4 GiB, so unwrapping needs a checkpoint and a nearest-representative rule. Write that
function first and property-test it before anything else.

**Test.** Beyond the course tests, write your own randomised harness: generate a random
byte stream, chop it into random overlapping segments, shuffle, duplicate, drop some, feed
them in, and assert the output stream equals the input. Run it 10^5 times with a printed
seed. Add a memory assertion so a reassembler that just buffers everything fails.

**Why.** After this week, "TCP guarantees an ordered byte stream" stops being a sentence
you repeat and becomes a data structure you have debugged. It is also the best available
practice at implementing a written specification exactly.

**Done looks like.** The course test suite passes. Your own fuzz harness passes 10^5
randomised cases. The seqno unwrap function has a property test covering the wrap boundary.

acceptance.text: The CS144 test suite for the byte stream, reassembler and receiver passes in full, with the output committed.
A self-written randomised reassembly fuzzer runs at least 10^5 cases with overlaps, duplicates and out-of-window segments, printing the seed on failure.
Peak reassembler memory is asserted to stay within capacity; a naive buffer-everything implementation is shown to fail that assertion.
`wrap`/`unwrap` between 32-bit seqno and 64-bit absolute index has a property test that crosses at least two 2^32 boundaries in both directions.
SYN and FIN are each shown, by test, to consume exactly one sequence number, including the case where FIN arrives in the same segment as data.
Build is clean with `-Wall -Wextra` and the test suite runs under ASan and UBSan.

levels.5: Passes the course tests and a 10^5-case randomised harness including segments that straddle the window edge.

weekly.title: CS144 part two: a TCP sender that fetches a real web page
weekly.brief:
Finish the stack. By the end of this week your own TCP implementation, running over a
TUN device on your laptop, should perform a three-way handshake with a real server on the
internet, issue an HTTP GET, and print the response.

**Build.** (1) `TCPSender` — outbound segmentation respecting the receiver's window,
tracking outstanding bytes, and the retransmission timer with exponential backoff, doubling
RTO on timeout and resetting it on a fresh ack. Handle the zero-window probe: when the
window is zero you must still send one byte, or the connection deadlocks forever. (2)
`TCPConnection` — the state machine tying sender and receiver together, including the
close sequence and TIME_WAIT with its `2*MSL` linger. (3) The adapter that carries your
segments over a TUN interface and out to the network.

**Then measure the protocol you built.** With `tcpdump` capturing your own stack:
- Show slow start in the wire trace: plot bytes in flight against time for a transfer and
  identify the exponential phase and the transition.
- Compute the bandwidth-delay product for a real path and show what happens when your
  window is smaller than it.
- Deliberately drop packets with `tc netem` at 1% and 5% and show the retransmission timer
  and the throughput collapse.
- Reproduce the Nagle-meets-delayed-ACK interaction and show the 40 ms stall in a capture.

**Why.** Very few working engineers have implemented TCP. Doing it, and then explaining a
`tcpdump` capture of your own implementation, is the credential this week buys. It is also
the foundation for the datacenter fabric and collectives material later.

**Done looks like.** A terminal recording of your stack fetching a page over the real
internet. Four captures with four annotated plots. A write-up that reads like a protocol
analysis, not a lab report.

acceptance.text: A recorded terminal session shows your stack completing a handshake with a real remote host and printing an HTTP response body.
A pcap of that exchange is committed and the write-up annotates SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK, the GET, and the FIN exchange by packet number.
The zero-window probe is tested: a receiver advertising a zero window is shown to be unblocked by a one-byte probe rather than deadlocking.
RTO doubling on consecutive timeouts and reset on a new ack are each demonstrated by a test and visible in a capture.

weekly.title: clox, then replace its garbage collector
weekly.brief:
Work through the second half of *Crafting Interpreters* and build `clox` — a bytecode
virtual machine for a real language, in C — then go past the book where the systems
learning actually is.

**Build.** The scanner, the single-pass compiler with Pratt parsing, the chunk and constant
pool, the stack VM with its dispatch loop, string interning, hash tables, closures with
upvalues, and classes with methods. Get it running the book's benchmark programs.

**Then extend, and this is the part that matters.** The book ships a naive mark-sweep
collector. Replace it:
1. Instrument the existing collector first. Record every pause: count, duration, distribution.
   You cannot claim an improvement you did not measure before.
2. Implement a generational collector — a copying young generation with a bump allocator and
   Cheney-style scavenging, promoting survivors to an old space collected by mark-sweep.
3. Add a write barrier so old-to-young pointers are tracked. Use a card table or a
   remembered set; state which and why. A missing barrier is the classic bug here and it
   produces corruption that only appears under load — write the test that catches it.
4. Benchmark: allocation-heavy, long-lived-data-heavy, and mixed workloads. Report pause
   distributions (p50/p99/max), not means, plus total collector time and peak RSS.

**Why.** After this you will have implemented, not read about, the generational hypothesis,
tri-colour marking, write barriers, and the throughput/pause trade. That is the difference
between "familiar with GC" and "has written one".

**Done looks like.** `clox` runs the book's test suite. The new collector runs the same
suite with identical output. Three benchmark workloads, pause distributions plotted for both
collectors, and an honest statement of which workload got worse.

weekly.title: xv6: page tables, traps, and copy-on-write fork
weekly.brief:
Do the memory half of MIT 6.1810 against the xv6-riscv kernel. You are modifying a real
(small) operating system, and the feedback loop is a kernel that either boots or panics.

**Labs.** (1) *pgtbl* — print a page table, add a per-process kernel page table, and map user
pages into it so the kernel can dereference user pointers directly. (2) *traps* — implement
backtrace by walking saved frame pointers, then `sigalarm`/`sigreturn`, which forces you to
understand exactly what a trapframe is and what must be saved and restored. (3) *cow* —
replace `fork`'s eager copy with copy-on-write: mark pages read-only, share them, and handle
the store page fault by allocating and copying, with a per-page reference count that is
correct under a fork storm. (4) *lazy* — lazy allocation for `sbrk`, so a page is only
allocated on first touch, including the case where the page is first touched by a syscall
in the kernel rather than by user code.

**Instrument it.** Add counters for minor faults, major faults, pages allocated and pages
freed, exposed through a new syscall. Then answer with data: how many physical pages does a
`fork`-heavy workload actually allocate with COW versus without? Where does the reference
count get decremented, and what happens if you forget one of the paths?

**Why.** Virtual memory is where the mental model of "a program running" is actually
implemented, and every later week — mmap, page cache, GPU unified memory, DMA — inherits its
vocabulary. Kernel work also teaches a specific discipline: there is no exception handler
above you.

**Done looks like.** `make grade` is green for all four labs. Your counters produce a table
showing COW's page saving on a workload you chose. A short write-up on the one bug that cost
you the most and how you found it.

weekly.title: The microarchitecture lab: make the hardware confess
weekly.brief:
Nine experiments, each of which measures one microarchitectural effect on your own
laptop and reports a number that matches (or refutes) the model.

1. **Cache hierarchy sizes.** A pointer-chase over a working set swept from 4 KiB to 64 MiB;
   plot latency per access and read the L1/L2/L3 sizes straight off the curve.
2. **Associativity.** Stride the chase by exactly the cache-set stride and show conflict
   misses appearing at the associativity boundary.
3. **TLB reach.** Sweep pages touched, with and without transparent huge pages, and show the
   second knee.
4. **Branch prediction.** A branch on random data versus sorted data over the same array;
   report the mispredict rate from the PMU and translate it into cycles using the measured
   misprediction penalty.
5. **False sharing.** Two threads incrementing counters in the same line versus padded;
   report the ratio and the coherence-related counter.
6. **Memory-level parallelism.** Independent chase chains 1 through 12 in flight; find where
   throughput saturates and infer the fill-buffer count.
7. **SIMD.** A scalar loop, an autovectorised loop, and an intrinsics loop, at three data

8. **Roofline.** Measure peak FLOP/s and peak bandwidth, then place five kernels (dot, axpy,
   stencil, small GEMM, transpose) on the roofline and predict each one's performance before
   measuring it.

weekly.title: BusTub P1: a buffer pool manager with LRU-K
weekly.brief:
Build CMU 15-445's first project by hand: the layer that owns every page a database
touches. The course explicitly prohibits coding agents on P1 and P2, and that is the right
instinct — this is the muscle.

**Build.** (1) An LRU-K replacer: track the last K access timestamps per frame, evict the
frame with the largest backward K-distance, and treat frames with fewer than K accesses as
having infinite distance, broken by earliest access. Support pinning, so an in-use frame is
never evicted. (2) A disk scheduler with a background worker and promise-based completion.
(3) The buffer pool manager itself: fetch, new, unpin, flush, delete, with a page table
mapping page ids to frames, a free list, dirty flags and pin counts. (4) Page guards
(RAII wrappers) so an unpin can never be forgotten on an early return.

**Get it right where it is hard.** Concurrency: multiple threads fetching, unpinning, and
evicting at once. Write a stress test that runs 8 threads for a million operations against a
pool of 16 frames and 10,000 pages, and asserts at the end that every page's contents are
what the last writer wrote and that the pin count is zero everywhere.

**Then measure.** Sweep pool size against a Zipf-distributed access pattern and plot hit
ratio. Compare LRU-K (K=2) against plain LRU on a scan-plus-hot-set workload — the workload
LRU is famously bad at — and report the difference. This is the same arithmetic you will use
again in the caching week.

**Why.** Every database's performance story starts here, and the buffer pool is the clearest
possible illustration that a cache's policy matters more than its size once the working set
exceeds it.

**Done looks like.** The course's own tests pass. Your stress test passes under ThreadSanitizer.
Two plots: hit ratio vs pool size, and LRU-K vs LRU on the scan workload.

weekly.title: BusTub P2: a concurrent B+ tree, and a cost model you can defend
weekly.brief:
Build the index. A B+ tree with real latch crabbing is the hardest single data structure
most engineers ever write, and it is the one that makes storage-engine conversations easy
forever after.

**Build.** Internal and leaf page layouts over the buffer pool from week 12; search, insert
with split and parent propagation, delete with borrow and merge, and an iterator for range
scans. Then concurrency: latch crabbing on the descent (acquire child, release parent once
the child is known safe), optimistic descent with read latches and a pessimistic retry when
the leaf turns out to be unsafe, and a defined order for the root latch that cannot deadlock.

**Then build a cost model.** Instrument the tree to count page reads and writes. Derive, on
paper, the height of a B+ tree for a given key size, page size and fill factor; predict the
page reads for a point lookup and a range scan of R rows; then measure and compare. Explain
the residual. Show empirically that pages settle at roughly 69% full under random insertion
and explain where that number comes from.

**Finally, the optimiser sketch.** Take a two-table join on a skewed dataset. Compute the
cost of hash join, sort-merge join and index nested-loop join by hand using your own
cardinality estimates; then run all three and report where your estimate was wrong and by
how much. The independence assumption will fail; quantify the failure.

**Why.** B+ tree plus cost estimation *is* the storage engine interview, and the
cardinality-estimation experiment is the cheapest way to internalise why query planners
misbehave.

**Done looks like.** Tests green including concurrency. A height/page-read prediction table
with measured values beside it. A join-cost table with your estimates, the real cardinalities,
and the resulting plan choice.

the subtle one — a leader may only commit an entry from a *previous* term indirectly, by
committing an entry from its own term; persistence of `currentTerm`, `votedFor` and the log
across crashes; and snapshotting with `InstallSnapshot` so the log does not grow forever.

**The bugs you will hit, and should write tests for.** Committing an entry replicated on a
majority but from an old term (the figure-8 scenario — this is the one that eats weeks).
Applying entries out of order because you released the lock between the commit-index update
and the apply. Resetting the election timer on the wrong events. Losing votes because the
RPC reply arrives after a term change. Log truncation that deletes entries a later leader
needed. Write each as a named regression test.

**Discipline.** Structured logging with a per-node prefix and a monotonically increasing
sequence, so a failing run produces a readable interleaving. Run the suite 500 times in a
loop and record the failure rate; a Raft that passes once is not a Raft.

**Why.** The research is unambiguous: this is one of the highest-value single artifacts
available in distributed systems, and next week you will break it on purpose.

**Done looks like.** 500 consecutive suite runs with zero failures, recorded. A written
account of the figure-8 bug in your own implementation, or, if you avoided it, a test proving
your implementation would have caught it.

weekly.title: A linearizable KV store on your Raft — then break it with Jepsen
weekly.brief:
Put a key-value store on top of last week's Raft, then attack it with an adversarial
consistency checker until you find a real violation, and fix it.

**Build.** A replicated KV store: `Get`, `Put`, `Append`, with client sessions and
deduplication so a retried request is not applied twice. Linearizable reads — either through
the log, or via a leader lease you must justify with clock-skew assumptions. Snapshot the
state machine so the Raft log can be truncated. Then shard it with a shard controller doing
live reconfiguration, so shards move between groups while clients keep operating.

**Break it.** Write a Jepsen test — or, if the Clojure tax is too high this week, a
Jepsen-style harness using Elle or Porcupine — that generates concurrent operations across
clients, injects faults (partitions, including a non-transitive partial partition, process
pauses via SIGSTOP, clock skew, and message reordering), records a history, and checks it for
linearizability. The point is to find something. Candidates: a stale read from a leader that
does not know it has been deposed, a duplicate apply after a client retry across a leader
change, a lost write during a shard migration.

**Report.** Write it as a Jepsen analysis: the claim under test, the workload, the
nemesis, the history that violates linearizability rendered as a diagram, the root cause, the
fix, and the re-run that passes.

**Why.** The career research is explicit that "I built it, then I broke it with an
adversarial checker, and here is the bug" is the credential. This week produces exactly that
sentence, backed by a document.

**Done looks like.** One reproducible linearizability violation with a committed history
file, a root-cause analysis, a fix, and a clean re-run.

acceptance.text: A KV store on Raft passes the course's linearizability tests including the unreliable-network and snapshot variants.
Client request deduplication is implemented and a test shows a retried request across a leader change applied exactly once.
A fault-injecting harness produces a recorded history file that a linearizability checker (Porcupine, Elle or Knossos) rejects — the violating history is committed.
The violation is root-caused to a specific code path, and the analysis names the invariant that was broken.
After the fix, the same harness with the same seed runs clean, and at least 100 further randomised runs pass.
The nemesis includes at least one partial (non-transitive) partition, and the write-up states why that class of fault is harder than a clean split.

levels.3: A violation found but not reproducible from a seed.
levels.5: A violation found, reproducible from a committed seed and history, and minimised to the smallest interleaving that still fails.

levels.5: Cause traced through the history to a specific line, with the broken invariant stated and a test that fails before the fix and passes after.

weekly.title: Cryptopals sets 1-3: break what you can already read
weekly.brief:
Do Cryptopals sets 1, 2 and 3 in a language you are not fluent in — Rust or Go — so
that the crypto is the only thing you are allowed to be slow at.

**Set 1 (basics).** Hex/base64, fixed XOR, single-byte XOR with English frequency scoring,
repeating-key XOR with Hamming-distance keysize detection, AES-ECB decryption, and ECB
detection. The lesson to actually extract: ECB leaks structure because it is a deterministic
codebook, and you can *see* it.

**Set 2 (block crypto).** PKCS#7 padding, CBC mode implemented by hand from an ECB
primitive, an ECB/CBC detection oracle, byte-at-a-time ECB decryption (both the simple and
the harder version with a random prefix), an ECB cut-and-paste attack on a profile encoder,
and CBC bit-flipping.

**Set 3 (block and stream crypto).** The CBC padding oracle — the single most instructive
attack in the whole set, because it turns a one-bit error signal into full plaintext
recovery. Then fixed-nonce CTR, breaking it statistically, and the MT19937 stream cipher
with seed recovery and state cloning.

**Discipline.** Every challenge gets a test asserting the recovered plaintext, so the whole
set is a suite you can re-run. Write a short note per challenge: what the attacker knows,
what oracle they have, and what property of the construction fails.

**Why.** The research calls this the best free security education in existence, and it is
the fastest route to the security mindset: you stop asking "is it encrypted" and start
asking "what does the attacker get to observe".

**Done looks like.** 24 challenges, 24 tests, 24 notes. A write-up on the padding oracle
with a diagram, because you will be asked about it.

acceptance.text: All 24 challenges of sets 1-3 have automated tests that assert the recovered key or plaintext, and the suite runs in CI.
CBC is implemented from an ECB primitive rather than by calling a library CBC mode; a test shows it interoperating with the library's implementation.
The padding-oracle attack recovers full plaintext for a message of at least three blocks and reports the number of oracle queries used.
Byte-at-a-time ECB decryption works in the harder random-prefix variant, and the prefix-length discovery step is explained.
Each challenge has a note stating the attacker's knowledge, the oracle, and the failing property.
Query counts are reported for the oracle attacks and compared against the theoretical expectation (128 per byte worst case for the padding oracle).

levels.3: Works on randomly generated messages of fixed length.
levels.5: Works on random messages of random length including block-aligned and single-block edge cases.

levels.5: CBC, CTR and PKCS#7 all hand-built and verified against a library implementation as an oracle.

weekly.title: Cryptopals sets 4-6, and a threat model for something you own
weekly.brief:
Finish the essential Cryptopals sets, then apply the mindset to a system you are actually
responsible for.

**Set 4 (stream crypto and randomness).** CTR seek and edit as an attack primitive, CTR
bitflipping, recovering a key from CBC where key equals IV, the SHA-1 and MD4
length-extension attacks (implement the hash yourself so you can set its internal state),
HMAC with an artificially insecure comparison, and the timing attack against it — including
the version with a 5 ms delay that forces you to do statistics rather than take one sample.

**Set 5 and 6 (public key).** Diffie-Hellman, then the parameter-injection MITM and the
malicious-`g` variants. RSA implemented from scratch, then the e=3 broadcast attack via the
Chinese Remainder Theorem, unpadded-message recovery, Bleichenbacher's e=3 signature forgery,
and DSA nonce recovery — both the biased-nonce and the repeated-nonce cases. If time is short,
prioritise: length extension, the timing attack, e=3 broadcast, and DSA nonce recovery.

**Then, the threat model.** Take the Whetstone app itself — a PHP/MySQL study app with
OAuth login, file uploads from a phone camera, an LLM-backed review worker, and an admin
panel. Produce: a data flow diagram with trust boundaries, STRIDE per element, an attack
tree for "attacker reads another learner's submissions", a prioritised mitigation list with
effort estimates, and a check of the design against the OWASP Top 10:2025. Include the
prompt-injection path explicitly: the LLM reviewer reads learner-supplied text and has tools.

**Why.** Sets 4-6 are where public-key intuition becomes real, and the threat model turns
security from a topic into a practice you apply to your own work.

**Done looks like.** Tests for every attempted challenge. A threat model document a security
engineer could review, with at least three findings you would actually fix.

weekly.title: A cache simulator, a real Redis, and an HTTP edge you can defend
weekly.brief:
Three layers of caching in one week, each with a measurement that changes a decision.

**Part 1 — the simulator.** Implement LRU, LFU, CLOCK, ARC, W-TinyLFU, S3-FIFO and SIEVE
behind one interface, plus Belady's optimal as the upper bound. Replay two traces: a Zipf
synthetic (sweep the skew parameter) and a real trace — use the access log from your week-2
`logkit` fixture, or a public CDN/Twitter cache trace. Plot hit ratio against cache size for
every policy, with Belady as the ceiling, and report each policy's distance from optimal.
Then show the scan-resistance case explicitly: a scan that ruins LRU and does not ruin
W-TinyLFU or S3-FIFO.

**Part 2 — Redis, actually measured.** Run Redis locally. Measure: the round-trip cost of
1,000 sequential `GET`s versus one pipelined batch; the memory cost per key for a small hash
under `listpack` encoding versus after it crosses the conversion threshold; what a `KEYS *`
on a million keys does to p99 latency of concurrent operations (use `redis-benchmark` in a
second terminal); and the difference between `volatile-lru` and `allkeys-lru` on a workload
where only some keys have TTLs. Then implement, in application code, a cache-aside path with
stampede protection via probabilistic early expiration, and demonstrate the thundering herd
with and without it.

**Part 3 — the HTTP layer.** Write a small origin that emits correct `Cache-Control`, `ETag`,
`Last-Modified` and `Vary`, and a client harness that proves each behaviour: a 304 round
trip, a `stale-while-revalidate` serve-then-refresh, a `Vary: Accept-Encoding` cache split,
and a private-versus-shared caching difference. Show the cache-key explosion that a careless
`Vary: User-Agent` causes.

**Why.** Caching is where most real systems' latency actually comes from, and the eviction
literature is a rare case where the newest simple algorithms genuinely beat the textbook one.

**Done looks like.** One hit-ratio-vs-size plot with eight curves and Belady on top. A Redis
measurement table. Four HTTP behaviours demonstrated by captured request/response pairs.

acceptance.text: Eight policies plus Belady's optimal run over the same traces through one interface, and the plot shows every policy's gap to optimal.
A scan workload is shown to collapse LRU's hit ratio while W-TinyLFU and S3-FIFO hold, with the scan length and hot-set size stated.
Pipelined versus sequential Redis round trips are measured on the same host, and the speedup is explained by RTT arithmetic rather than asserted.
Per-key memory is measured before and after the listpack conversion threshold, using `MEMORY USAGE`, with the configured threshold stated.
The thundering herd is demonstrated with a measured origin-request spike, then suppressed by probabilistic early expiration, with both traces shown.
Four HTTP caching behaviours are each demonstrated by a committed pair of request and response headers, and the `Vary` cache-key explosion is quantified.

weekly.title: A training-data pipeline: Parquet, Iceberg, watermarks and dedup
weekly.brief:
Build the pipeline that produces the corpus you will later train on, and make every
stage reproducible and idempotent. Everything runs locally: DuckDB, PyArrow, PySpark in local
mode, and a Kafka or Redpanda container. No cluster, no cloud bill.

**Batch side.** Ingest a public raw text corpus slice (a Common Crawl WET sample, or
Wikipedia dumps) into Parquet. Then: choose row-group size and compression deliberately and
measure the effect on scan time and file size; demonstrate predicate pushdown and data
skipping by comparing bytes read with and without a min/max-friendly sort order; register the
tables in Iceberg and demonstrate schema evolution, time travel to a prior snapshot, and a
`MERGE` for an incremental model. Then deliberately create the small-files problem — 10,000
tiny files — measure the planning and scan cost, compact, and measure again.

**Quality and dedup.** Implement MinHash + LSH near-duplicate detection yourself: shingle,
hash, band, bucket, candidate pairs, verify by true Jaccard. Tune bands and rows for a target
threshold and *derive* the S-curve rather than guessing. Report duplicates found, precision
against a hand-labelled sample of 100 pairs, and runtime. Add the heuristic quality filters
(length, symbol ratio, repetition) and report how much data each removes.

**Stream side.** A Kafka topic of synthetic events with deliberately late and out-of-order
arrivals. Build a windowed aggregation with an event-time watermark derived from the observed
lateness distribution — not a guessed constant. Show what a too-aggressive watermark drops
and what a too-lax one costs in state size and latency. Implement the read-process-write loop
with Kafka transactions and prove exactly-once *effects* by killing the consumer mid-batch
and showing no duplicate output.

**Why.** This is the pipeline every ML training run silently depends on, and deduplication in
particular is one of the highest-leverage data decisions in language modelling.

**Done looks like.** One `make all` that rebuilds every artifact from raw input. A table of
measured effects for each design choice. A dedup report with precision numbers.

acceptance.text: `make all` rebuilds every output from raw inputs on a clean checkout, and re-running it produces byte-identical outputs (idempotence asserted by checksum).
Row-group size and compression codec are swept, and scan time and file size are reported for at least three combinations with the chosen configuration justified.
Bytes read with and without data skipping are reported from the engine's own metrics, not estimated.
MinHash LSH is implemented from scratch; the band/row choice is derived from the target Jaccard threshold and the S-curve is plotted.
Dedup precision is measured against at least 100 hand-labelled candidate pairs and reported with the false-positive examples shown.
The watermark is derived from the measured lateness distribution, and drop rate versus state size is reported for at least three watermark settings.
A consumer killed mid-batch is shown to produce no duplicate downstream effects across at least ten kill/restart cycles.

weekly.title: A design document, and the slice of it you actually build and load-test
weekly.brief:
Produce the artifact senior engineers are actually judged on: a design document with
numbers in it, plus a working slice that proves the numbers were not invented.

**Part 1 — the document.** Pick a system with real constraints — a submission-and-review
pipeline for this study app at 100k users, or an inference gateway serving a quantised 7B
model to 2,000 concurrent users in India. The document must contain: requirements
(functional and non-functional, with the non-functional ones as numbers); a capacity
estimate derived from DAU to QPS to storage to bandwidth, with every step shown and the cost
in INR per month; an API sketch; a data model; the queueing analysis (Little's Law,
utilisation target and the reason headroom is not waste, fan-out tail amplification); an
availability analysis; SLIs, SLOs and an error budget with burn-rate alert thresholds; a
migration plan; and an explicit list of three alternatives considered and rejected, each with
the condition that would flip the decision.

**Part 2 — the slice.** Build the smallest thing that lets you test the riskiest number. For
the inference gateway that is a request queue with continuous batching simulated against a
measured single-request latency curve; for the submission pipeline it is the queue plus the
worker plus the idempotency key path. Then load-test it: k6 or vegeta, open-model load
generation (constant arrival rate, not closed-loop) so you do not fall into coordinated
omission. Plot latency percentiles against offered load, find the knee, and compare it against
the M/M/1 or M/M/c curve you predicted.

**Part 3 — the review.** Post the document publicly and ask for critique. Record the critique
and your response in a revision section. Changing your mind well, in public, with the reason
stated, is the behaviour the level actually rewards.

**Why.** Writing is the primary instrument past senior. This week produces a writing sample
with arithmetic in it, which is exactly what a hiring committee reads.

**Done looks like.** A document a stranger could implement from. A load-test result that
either confirms or refutes your capacity estimate, with the refutation kept in if it happened.

acceptance.text: The capacity estimate derives QPS, storage, bandwidth and monthly INR cost from stated assumptions, with every arithmetic step visible and each assumption labelled as measured, cited or guessed.
The load generator uses an open model (fixed arrival rate) and the write-up states why closed-loop generation would understate tail latency.
Latency percentiles are plotted against offered load and the knee is identified; the measured knee is compared against the queueing model's prediction.
SLOs are stated with an error budget and at least two burn-rate alert thresholds with their detection windows computed.
Three rejected alternatives are documented, each with the specific condition under which the decision would flip.
At least one external critique is recorded, with your response and any resulting revision marked in the document's history.

levels.5: Numbers present, each traced to a user-visible consequence, and the measurement method for each is defined.

levels.5: Derivation shown step by step with every assumption labelled by provenance and a sensitivity note on the one that matters most.

weekly.title: A transformer from scratch, trained on a laptop
weekly.brief:
Write a decoder-only transformer with no reference to an existing implementation while
you write it, train it on a small corpus on CPU or a free Colab T4, and verify every
component against an independent implementation afterwards.

**Build, in this order, each with a shape and gradient test before moving on.** Tokenizer:
train BPE yourself on the corpus from week 19 (merges, the pre-tokenisation split, byte-level
fallback) and show a round-trip on text containing emoji, code and numbers. Embedding and
weight-tied unembedding. RoPE, implemented from the rotation definition — then verify the
relative-position property numerically: `q_m . k_n` should depend only on `m - n`. Causal
multi-head attention, then GQA with a configurable KV-head count. RMSNorm, pre-norm
placement. SwiGLU with the expansion ratio chosen and justified. The residual stream. A KV
cache for generation.

**Verify.** Load GPT-2 small's weights into your architecture (adapting for the differences
you must document) and check that your forward pass reproduces HuggingFace's logits to within
1e-4. If it does not, the difference is a bug in your understanding and finding it is the
week's real lesson.

**Then compute, not recall.** For your config, count parameters exactly and check against the
model's own parameter count. Derive FLOPs per token and check the 6N approximation against
your exact count, stating where the approximation loses. Compute attention FLOPs as a
fraction of total at three sequence lengths and find the crossover where the quadratic term
dominates. Compute KV-cache size in bytes for MHA, MQA and GQA at your config.

**Train.** A small model on your corpus with a proper warmup-plus-cosine schedule, gradient
clipping by global norm, and a held-out loss curve. Report tokens seen, final loss and
perplexity, and sample text.

**Why.** Everything in the frontier-ML half of the curriculum is this object. Building it
once with the arithmetic checked is the difference between using a transformer and knowing one.

acceptance.text: Your forward pass reproduces HuggingFace GPT-2 small logits to within 1e-4 max absolute difference on at least 10 prompts, with the check committed as a test.

weekly.title: The GEMM ladder: from naive CUDA to within a stated fraction of cuBLAS
weekly.brief:
Climb the kernel ladder on a free Colab or Kaggle T4, and report every rung against
cuBLAS. Total spend: zero rupees. Optional: a few hundred rupees of spot A100 time to see
whether your conclusions transfer.

**The ladder.** (0) Vector add, to establish the bandwidth ceiling and confirm you can
measure. (1) Naive GEMM, one thread per output element — compute achieved GFLOP/s and
arithmetic intensity and show why it is memory-bound. (2) Global-memory coalescing: change
only the thread-to-element mapping and report the speedup. (3) Shared-memory tiling; derive
the intensity improvement from the tile size before measuring it. (4) Register tiling, each
thread computing a small output tile. (5) Bank-conflict removal: compute the conflict degree
for your access pattern, then fix it by padding and again by swizzling, and report both. (6)
Double buffering / `cp.async` to overlap the global load with compute. (7) Tensor cores via
`wmma` for fp16 accumulate-fp32, with a numerical accuracy comparison against the fp32 path.

**Also do the reduction ladder** (Harris's seven rungs) and the transpose ladder (naive,
tiled, padded) — they are short and they teach divergence and bank conflicts in isolation.

**Then Triton.** Reimplement the tiled GEMM and a fused softmax in Triton, autotune over
block sizes, `num_warps` and `num_stages`, and compare against your CUDA versions and against
`torch.compile`'s generated kernel. State where Triton stops being able to express what you
want.

**Report properly.** For every rung: achieved GFLOP/s, percentage of cuBLAS, achieved
bandwidth, occupancy, and the Nsight Compute Speed-of-Light section. Roofline-place every
kernel. State the GPU, clocks, and whether they were locked.

**Why.** The kernel ladder is the standard entry credential for GPU work, and the discipline
of predicting each rung's gain before measuring it is what makes the knowledge transferable.

acceptance.text: Every rung is benchmarked against cuBLAS on the same shapes and dtype, and the result is reported as a percentage of cuBLAS with the shapes stated.
Correctness is checked against a CPU reference within a tolerance derived from the accumulation precision, for every kernel including the tensor-core one.

Bank-conflict degree is computed by hand for the shared-memory access pattern and confirmed against the profiler's conflict counter.
The Triton GEMM's autotuned configuration is reported, and the comparison with the CUDA version and torch.compile is on identical shapes and dtypes.
GPU model, clock state, and whether clocks were locked are reported, and run-to-run variance is given for the headline numbers.

weekly.title: An inference engine: paged KV, continuous batching, and int4 weights
weekly.brief:
Build a small but real LLM serving engine around your week-21 transformer (or a 1-3B
open model), and make every performance claim a measurement.

**Build.** (1) Separate prefill and decode paths, and measure each: prefill is
compute-bound, decode is memory-bound, and you should be able to show it on a roofline with
your own numbers. (2) A paged KV cache: fixed-size blocks, a block table per sequence, and a
free-block allocator. Measure fragmentation against a naive contiguous allocator at the same
memory budget and report how many more concurrent sequences you fit. (3) Continuous batching:
a scheduler that admits new requests at every decode step rather than waiting for the batch to
drain. Report throughput and p99 time-to-first-token against static batching under a Poisson
arrival process. (4) Chunked prefill so a long prompt does not stall the decode queue; show
the p99 TTFT improvement. (5) Prefix caching for a shared system prompt; measure the saving.
(6) Speculative decoding with a small draft model: measure the acceptance rate and check the
measured speedup against the expected value computed from acceptance rate and draft length.

**Quantise.** Implement weight-only int8 and int4 group quantisation yourself: the affine
map, group size, and a calibration pass choosing the clipping range. Report, for group sizes
32/64/128: perplexity on a held-out set, model bytes, and decode tokens/sec. Then implement
one of SmoothQuant's activation-scale migration or AWQ's activation-aware scaling and show
whether it recovers the perplexity gap. Also quantise the KV cache to int8 and report the
quality/memory trade.

**Why.** Serving economics is where most ML systems work actually lives, and the arithmetic
here — bytes per token, acceptance rate, batch size versus latency — is directly interview
material and directly job material.

**Done looks like.** A table with rows for each technique and columns for tokens/sec, p99
TTFT, memory, and perplexity delta. No row without a measurement.

acceptance.text: Prefill and decode are measured separately and each is placed on a roofline built from your own measured peaks, showing the compute-bound/memory-bound split.
Paged KV is compared against contiguous allocation at an identical memory budget, reporting concurrent sequences served and wasted bytes.
Continuous batching is compared against static batching under a Poisson arrival process at three arrival rates, reporting throughput and p99 TTFT.
Speculative decoding reports measured acceptance rate, and the observed speedup is compared against the value predicted from acceptance rate and draft length.
Int4 group quantisation is implemented from the affine map; perplexity, bytes and tokens/sec are reported for group sizes 32, 64 and 128.
An activation-aware method (SmoothQuant or AWQ) is implemented and its perplexity recovery over naive round-to-nearest is quantified.
Quantised outputs are validated for correctness beyond perplexity: at least one task-level check, with the sampling seed fixed.

weekly.title: A nanoGPT speedrun reproduction with one documented improvement
weekly.brief:
Reproduce a published training speedrun exactly, then make one measured, documented
improvement. The career research is explicit that reproducing a hard result in public, and
competing on a legible leaderboard, is among the strongest credentials available without a
PhD or a lab affiliation.

**Stage 1 — reproduce.** Take a specific `modded-nanogpt` speedrun record (pin the commit)
or the `nanochat` speedrun. Rent 8xH100 spot for the run — roughly USD 15-50, so budget about
INR 4,500 including a failed first attempt, which you will have. Before renting, do a full dry
run on a free Colab T4 at 1/100 scale so that every bug that is not about scale is already
fixed. Reproduce the reported metric. If you cannot reproduce it, that is a result: document
exactly where you diverged and by how much.

**Stage 2 — improve one thing.** One variable. Candidates that are cheap to test and honest
to report: a change to the learning-rate schedule; a change to the Muon optimiser's
Newton-Schulz iteration count; logit soft-capping; a different value-embedding scheme; a
tokenizer trained on a cleaner corpus (yours, from week 19); attention-window schedule. Design
the experiment first: hypothesis, the single variable, the metric, the number of seeds, and
the decision rule stated before the run.

**Stage 3 — report like a researcher.** Baseline and treatment with seed variance, not two
single runs. State the compute spent. State what you would need to check the result at larger
scale, and be explicit that a result at this scale may not hold at another. Include the
ablations that did not work.

**Why.** This is the portfolio piece the career dossier names directly: a public, legible,
competitive reproduction with a measured delta. It is also the cheapest way to practise the
experimental discipline the rest of the curriculum only discusses.

**Done looks like.** A reproduction within a stated tolerance of the published number, one
improvement with seed variance, a public write-up, and — if the improvement holds — an issue
or pull request on the upstream repository.

acceptance.text: The baseline reproduction is run at the pinned upstream commit and the achieved metric is reported against the published one, with any gap explained.
A scaled-down dry run on free hardware is completed and documented before any paid compute is spent.
The improvement changes exactly one variable, and the hypothesis, metric and decision rule are recorded in git before the run.
Baseline and treatment are each run with at least three seeds, and the result is reported as a distribution with an effect size, not two point estimates.
Total compute spent is reported in GPU-hours and INR, including failed runs.
At least one negative result is reported — an idea tried that did not help — with its measurement.
The write-up states the scale at which the claim was tested and explicitly declines to extrapolate beyond it.

levels.3: Metric close to published; deviations unexamined.

levels.5: Three or more seeds with spread reported, an effect size stated, and the decision rule applied as pre-registered even when it goes against the hypothesis.

levels.5: Every arm run is reported with its numbers, including the ones abandoned, and the abandonment criterion is stated.

weekly.title: A pipelined RV32I core, verified in cocotb, that runs your own C
weekly.brief:
Design a RISC-V processor in SystemVerilog, verify it with a Python testbench under
Verilator, and run a C program you compiled on it. Everything here is free and runs on your
laptop; the FPGA board is optional and costs INR 3,829.

**Prerequisite drills.** Finish HDLBits (about 180 graded exercises, 30-50 hours) before this
week if you have not already — it is the single highest-value RTL resource and it will surface
every misconception you have about combinational versus sequential logic. Then build a UART
transmitter and receiver with a cocotb testbench against a numpy reference model, and put it
in CI. From that point every module you write gets a testbench. That discipline *is* the skill.

**Build.** (1) A single-cycle RV32I core first: register file, ALU, immediate decode for all
six formats, branch unit, load/store with sub-word alignment. Pass the `riscv-tests` ISA
suite under Verilator. (2) Then pipeline it into five stages with a proper hazard unit:
forwarding from EX/MEM and MEM/WB, a load-use interlock that stalls exactly one cycle, and
branch resolution with flush. Pass `riscv-tests` again — the pipelined version will fail
tests the single-cycle one passed, and finding out which and why is the point. (3) Add a
CSR subset and machine-mode trap handling for at least `ecall` and an illegal instruction.

**Verify like an engineer, not a hobbyist.** cocotb testbenches with a Python instruction-set
simulator as the golden model, running randomised instruction streams generated with
constraints (hypothesis is fine) and comparing architectural state after every instruction.
Concurrent SVA assertions for the pipeline invariants: no two writes to the same register in
a cycle, no forwarding from a bubble, no branch resolved twice. Functional coverage on
instruction type crossed with hazard type; report the coverage number. Then formally verify
with SymbiYosys, ideally against `riscv-formal`.

**Measure.** Report CPI on a benchmark (Dhrystone or a hand-written loop), the stall and flush
counts by cause, and the synthesised Fmax and LUT/FF usage from Yosys or Vivado.

**Why.** This is the project where the abstraction stack collapses into one thing you
understand: your C, your compiler's assembly, your ISA, your datapath.

acceptance.text: The pipelined core passes the full `riscv-tests` RV32I ISA suite under Verilator, with output committed.
A C program compiled with the RISC-V GCC toolchain runs on the core and produces correct output via a memory-mapped UART or a testbench hook.
A cocotb testbench compares architectural state against a Python ISS after every instruction for at least 10^6 randomly generated instructions, with the seed printed.
The load-use interlock stalls exactly one cycle and a directed test proves it; a test also proves forwarding removes the stall in the non-load case.
Functional coverage of instruction type crossed with hazard type is reported as a percentage, with the uncovered bins listed.
At least three concurrent SVA assertions on pipeline invariants are present and are shown to fire on a deliberately injected bug.
CPI, stall counts by cause, flush counts, synthesised Fmax and resource usage are all reported for a named benchmark.

weekly.title: An 8x8 int8 systolic array: RTL, Timeloop model, and a LibreLane run to GDSII
weekly.brief:
The capstone. Design a matrix multiply accelerator, model it quantitatively, push it
through an open-source ASIC flow to a real layout, and write the whole thing up. This is the
artifact a hiring manager in accelerator architecture will actually read.

**Part 1 — the RTL.** An 8x8 weight-stationary int8 systolic array: a PE with a MAC and a
register, double-buffered SRAM tiles for weights and activations, an accumulator bank with
enough width that no realistic accumulation overflows (derive the width, do not guess), and a
controller doing load-weights / stream-activations / drain. Verify in cocotb against a numpy
matmul, bit-exact, for random matrices and for the edge cases: matrices smaller than the
array, matrices that do not tile evenly, and an accumulation designed to overflow if your
width arithmetic was wrong. Report fill and drain cycles and show why small batches waste
the array. Then parameterise to 16x16 and report how LUT, DSP and BRAM usage scales.

**Part 2 — model it.** Build a Timeloop + Accelergy specification of your architecture, and
run a mapspace search across weight-stationary, output-stationary and row-stationary
dataflows for the layers of a real small network. Report bytes moved per MAC for each
dataflow and cross-check the best mapping against SCALE-Sim. Produce a roofline for your
accelerator and place the layers on it. Then answer the question the model exists to answer:
for your array size and SRAM budget, which layers are bound by the array and which by the
memory system, and what is the smallest change that moves the bottleneck?

**Part 3 — take it to silicon.** Push one block — the PE, or a 4x4 array — through LibreLane
to GDSII on sky130. Read the timing, area and power reports and understand every number. View
it in KLayout. Report the achieved clock, the cell count, the area in square micrometres, and
where the critical path is. This single exercise gives you most of the physical-design
literacy an architect needs.

**Part 4 — write it up.** The write-up is the portfolio piece, not the code. Architecture,
the dataflow decision with the model that justified it, the verification strategy, the

Report which optimisations survived and which broke on wavefront 64 versus warp 32. Then reason, with your data, about why performance portability is genuinely hard and what a portability layer can and cannot do.

acceptance.text: A CUDA kernel ported to HIP and run on AMD, with a per-optimisation survival report.
A written analysis of one optimisation that had to change for wavefront 64, with the reason.

daily.public_artifact: Commit `portability/`.
daily.stretch: Express the same kernel in Triton and measure whether it closes the portability gap between the two vendors.

daily.title: Arithmetic hardware, built and timed
daily.brief: Implement a ripple-carry adder, a carry-lookahead adder, a carry-save adder tree, and an array multiplier in SystemVerilog. Verify each in cocotb against a Python reference. Then synthesise and compare their logic depth and area, confirming the log-depth advantage of carry-lookahead and the compression advantage of the carry-save tree.

acceptance.text: Four arithmetic units verified in cocotb against a Python reference.
Synthesised depth and area compared, confirming carry-lookahead's log-depth and the carry-save tree's compression.

concepts: The full adder and ripple-carry delay
Carry-lookahead: generate, propagate, and log depth
daily.public_artifact: Commit `arithmetic-hw/`; feeds weeks 25-26.
daily.stretch: Implement Booth radix-4 recoding for the multiplier and show the partial-product count halving.

daily.title: Chiplets, packaging and the cost of area
daily.brief: Compute die yield from a defect density and die area (the negative-binomial or Poisson model), and show why chiplets beat one large die past a size threshold. Then compare 2.5D interposers, 3D stacking and UCIe die-to-die links on bandwidth and cost, and state where advanced packaging is the enabler for a modern accelerator's memory bandwidth.

acceptance.text: Die yield computed from defect density and area, with the chiplet crossover threshold derived.
A comparison of 2.5D, 3D and UCIe on bandwidth and cost, with the packaging choice for an HBM-fed accelerator justified.

concepts: Die yield and the cost of area
Collective bandwidth as the real cluster metric
daily.public_artifact: Commit `packaging/`.
daily.stretch: Compute the cost per good die for a monolithic versus a chiplet design at three yield levels and find the break-even area.

daily.title: Inference sampling, characterised
daily.brief: Implement temperature, top-k, top-p (nucleus) and min-p sampling, and characterise each: how the effective vocabulary size changes with the parameter, how repetition and coherence trade off, and where each fails (top-k at a flat distribution, top-p at a peaked one). Verify the Gumbel-max equivalence to temperature sampling empirically.

acceptance.text: Four samplers implemented with the effective-vocabulary-versus-parameter curve for each.
The Gumbel-max trick shown empirically equivalent to temperature sampling over many draws.

concepts: Sampling: temperature, top-k, top-p and min-p
The Gumbel-max trick and temperature sampling
Cross-entropy as the LLM loss, mechanically

daily.stretch: Measure how each sampler affects a downstream task's pass@k and find the parameter that maximises it.

daily.title: Chain replication and leases
daily.brief: Implement chain replication (writes down the chain, reads from the tail) and compare its consistency and throughput profile against quorum replication. Then implement leases with fencing tokens and demonstrate the split-brain scenario a naive lease allows and how a fencing token prevents a stale leader's write from being applied.

acceptance.text: Chain replication implemented and compared against quorum on consistency and throughput.
A fencing token shown rejecting a stale leader's write that a naive lease would have allowed.
